query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an appropriate thermomechanical processing route that refines and hierarchically re-organizes the inherited eutectic lamellar structure of an EHEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) will simultaneously improve its yield strength and ductility compared to as‐cast samples.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (EHEA) with a lamellar microstructure combining a soft FCC phase and a hard BCC or intermetallic phase.
generation.intervention: Apply severe cold rolling (e.g., ~70% thickness reduction) followed by a controlled annealing (sub‐recrystallization or intermediate temperature anneal) treatment aimed at creating an ultrafine-grained, hierarchical duplex lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: Quasi-static tensile testing at room temperature, where the microstructure is stable and the lamellar architecture is retained.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchically refined duplex lamellar microstructure with ultrafine-grained regions and increased interphase boundaries that promote dislocation storage and act as barriers to crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The refined hierarchical structure induces a two-hierarchical constraint effect and facilitates a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This mitigates strain localization while providing additional barriers to dislocation motion, thereby simultaneously enhancing strength (via grain boundary and phase constraint strengthening) and ductility (by allowing better strain partitioning and delaying failure).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the processed alloy is expected to exhibit a marked increase in yield strength along with improved ductility (e.g., both increased by on the order of tens of percent), although the precise gains depend on processing parameters.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic HEA with its native lamellar microstructure.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold under room-temperature, quasi-static loading conditions in eutectic HEAs that inherit a lamellar composite microstructure; outcomes may vary if the alloy composition or processing parameters fall outside the designed window.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements are uncertain and will depend on specific processing details (e.g., degree of deformation, annealing temperature/time) and the particular EHEA composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of an EHEA such as AlCoCrFeNi2.1: one set in the as-cast state and one set subjected to severe cold rolling (~70% reduction) followed by a controlled annealing treatment designed to yield a hierarchical duplex lamellar structure. Characterize the microstructure using SEM/TEM to confirm lamellar refinement and hierarchical organization. Then perform identical quasi-static tensile tests at room temperature on both sets.
measurements: Microstructural features (grain size, lamellar spacing, phase distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically processed samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase (e.g., >10% improvement) in both yield strength and ductility relative to the as-cast baseline, or if the refined hierarchical microstructure is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. He et al. [] designed a pseudo binary alloy, i.e., the CoCrFeNi HEA with a single FCC solid-solution phase as the base alloy and Nb as the additional element. Such simple pseudo binary method was followed by Jin et al. []. First, they chose one HEA with a single solid-solution phase and one stable binary intermetallic compound. After that, they obtained the HEA with dual phase by mixing the two phases. To ensure the formation of an eutectic structure, three conditions were proposed: (1) The single solid-solution phase should be stable enough without any segregation and precipitation; (2) the binary intermetallic compound should be stable from room temperature to its melting point; (3) the intermetallic compound must have the most negative mixing of enthalpy among all the binary combinations in the alloy. With CoCrFeNi2, Co2CrFeNi and CoCrFe2Ni as the HEAs with a single FCC solid-solution phase and NiAl as the binary intermetallic compound, they found three new EHEAs.
